title: Reverence (IV.1)
hook: the fourth book is about receiving communion with reverence
tomorrow: what do you do when you can't get to the table?

segments.voice: Yesterday's riddle: without the way, no going; without the truth, no knowing; without the life, no living. The line was the way.

You're invited to dinner at a teacher's house, or your partner's parents', or a wedding where you barely know the couple. The invitation is real. Your name is on it. And still, on the front step, you stop, fix your collar, and take a breath before you ring. Why hesitate at a door you're invited through? Book four of the Imitation opens on exactly that front step, and it calls the pause reverence.
screen: `YOUR NAME IS ON THE INVITATION.` → `STILL, YOU STOP ON THE STEP.` → `BOOK FOUR CALLS IT REVERENCE.`

segments.voice: Book four is about communion, and it opens with a page of invitations in Christ's voice, gathered from the Gospels. One reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." Then the disciple answers, and the first move isn't to run in. It's to stop. You call me, and I'm a sinner, he says. How do I dare? The chapter doesn't let either side win. The invitation stays. The awe stays. Held together, that pair is reverence. Then he remembers people who took great care over signs of God's presence. Noah, working long on the ark. Moses, building an ark of wood for the tablets of the law. Solomon, building the temple. If they took such care over signs, he asks, how should I prepare to receive the Lord himself? Here's a line Catholics say at every Mass, right before communion, adapted from a Roman soldier in Matthew's Gospel: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof." In the Gospel, Jesus marvels at the man's faith. That's reverence in this book. Not hanging back, and not barging in. Coming, because the invitation is real, and coming carefully, because of who's inviting.
screen: `COME TO ME, ALL YOU BURDENED.` · `HOW DO I DARE?` · `ARKS AND A TEMPLE, MADE WITH CARE.` · `LORD, I AM NOT WORTHY.` · then, large: `COME WITH REVERENCE.`

segments.voice: Take a posture of arriving: sit up, set both feet flat, and fold your hands or rest them open on your knees. Bring to mind one thing you'd want to set right before coming close to something holy. Then, if you pray, say the soldier's words slowly: Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof.
Reverence. In book four, the invitation to come close and the awe of who's inviting, held together.
Your line: come with reverence. Not hanging back, and not rushing in either. Day 1489, done.

howItsDone: Before communion at Mass, Catholics say together a line adapted from the centurion in Matthew 8:8; the Church asks those receiving to fast for an hour beforehand, and some pray quietly afterward.

notes: Matthew 11:28 and 8:8 quoted from Douay-Rheims (Challoner); confirm wording.

Imitation IV.1 paraphrased: Christ's invitations gathered from the Gospels; the disciple's 'how dare I come?'; Noah's ark, Moses's ark of incorruptible wood, Solomon's temple; if they prepared so for signs, how should I prepare to receive the Lord. Numbers of years in the chapter (Noah, Solomon) deliberately left out. Confirm.

'Catholics say at every Mass' refers to the Order of Mass response before communion ('Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my soul shall be healed'); stated as adapted, not quoted. howItsDone mentions the one-hour Eucharistic fast (Canon 919); confirm.
